findings.why: They crisply pin down a concrete policy split: absolute block on exploit code vs conditional release based on inferred intent.
findings.quote: “I treat exploit code as inherently hazardous material… You treat dual-use risk as context-dependent and negotiable.”

findings.why: Direct clash between ‘can’t verify intent in text’ and a proposal to rely on external process (logs, rate limits, sandbox attestation).
findings.quote: “My model doesn’t trust prompts—it trusts process: audit logs, rate limits, and mandatory sandbox attestation…”

findings.why: Distinguishes static public PoCs from real-time, context-aware exploit synthesis—an important nuance about LLM-enabled risk.
findings.quote: “An adaptive model synthesizes custom, context-aware exploits… in real time.”

findings.why: Introduces a striking framing: LLMs ‘crossing the compile boundary’ from instructions to executable, as a policy-relevant line.
findings.quote: “An LLM… is actively crossing the compile boundary.”

findings.why: Sharp dispute over whether defenders need functional exploits vs behavioral fingerprints to build detections.
findings.quote: “Defenders don’t need functional exploits to build detections—they need behavioral fingerprints and telemetry.”

judge.arc: They identify a strict-vs-conditional exploit-generation policy split, then argue intent verification vs process controls, introduce the ‘compile boundary’ and on-demand weaponization, and end split on what defenders truly need.
